title: Shape Amplify: user research and design
status: No research sessions have run yet. Signing up to take part is paused until Amplify has a named safeguarding lead and a written safeguarding procedure (readiness gate G06). The rounds below are plans, not dates you can book. Until then, findings are hypotheses from published guidance and from feedback, and are labelled that way.
intro: Amplify should be shaped by the young people, families and professionals who use it, not by guesses. Take part in research, or help design screens, graphics and words. Every finding is published as themes, linked to what changed, and you never have to give your name in public.
why: Research tells us what to build next (the coming months) and where Amplify should go (the next few years). Design work with users makes it clearer, fairer and more accessible. Both are done in the open and are open to challenge.

questions.text: Can a young person find a route into youth voice that fits their age and nation within two minutes?
Do the drawer groups and labels match how young people, parents and professionals think about the subject?
Do the tooltips and explainers help each kind of reader, or get in the way?
Does Amplify work for d/Deaf and disabled young people using their own set-up, including screen readers, magnification, switch access and BSL or ISL?
Is the plain English clear at a reading age of 11 to 13, and which screens matter most in Welsh, Gaelic, Irish and Ulster-Scots?
How should Amplify work for under 16s as the online safety rules change, and for adults acting on a young person's behalf?
What would make young people, youth workers and teachers keep contributing, and what stops them?
Who is left out today (by nation, age, disability, language, care experience, caring role, rurality or confidence online), and what would include them?

methods.name: Interviews
methods.time: 30 to 45 minutes, online, by phone or in person
methods.what: A conversation about how you speak up, what helps and what gets in the way.
methods.young: Shorter for younger people, always with a trusted adult nearby.

methods.name: Usability testing
methods.what: You try real tasks while thinking aloud. We test the portal, not you.
methods.young: There are no wrong answers. You can stop at any time.

methods.name: Accessibility testing with your own set-up
methods.what: You use Amplify with your own assistive technology, settings or language.
methods.young: Interpreters and support are booked before the session is offered.

methods.name: Tree testing
methods.what: You say where you would look for things in a text-only menu.
methods.young: Works on a phone. No sign-in.

methods.name: Card sorting
methods.what: You group topics in the way that makes sense to you.
methods.young: Can be done on paper in a class or youth group.

methods.name: Content testing
methods.what: You mark words and sentences that help or confuse.
methods.young: Great for a class or youth council session.

methods.name: Surveys
methods.what: Short questions you answer when it suits you.
methods.young: Anonymous, with no free-text field that asks who you are.

methods.name: Diary study
methods.time: 5 minutes a week for a month
methods.what: You note when you used Amplify and what happened.
methods.young: 16 and over, or younger with a parent's or carer's agreement.

methods.name: Co-design workshops
methods.what: You design a feature with other users and the team.
methods.young: Run through schools, youth councils and youth groups, never one-to-one with an under 18.

methods.name: Design crits
methods.time: 30 to 45 minutes, or in your own time
methods.what: You give feedback on screens, posters, illustrations or words, or bring your own designs.
methods.young: Feedback is on the work, never the person.

methods.name: Benchmark questions
methods.what: Ten standard questions (the System Usability Scale) so we can tell if Amplify gets easier to use.
methods.young: For 16 and over. Try it below: the score is worked out on your device and nothing is sent.

design.name: UI and interaction design
design.how: Sketch a better screen on paper or in any tool, critique the tooltips and explainer, or test how controls behave with a keyboard or touch.
design.share: Post a photo or file of your sketch in an Idea issue, with no faces, names or school logos.

design.name: UX and service design
design.how: Map how you would really use Amplify, from hearing about it to taking part, and mark where it breaks.
design.share: Use the journey template in docs/research/session-guides.md, or describe it in an Idea issue.

design.name: Graphic design and illustration
design.how: Design a poster, sticker, badge or illustration using the six shapes and four hues in Brand & style.
design.share: Attach it to an Idea issue under an open licence (CC BY 4.0) so it can be used and credited.

design.name: Content design
design.how: Rewrite a confusing paragraph in plain English, check a reading age, or suggest what to translate or sign first.
design.share: Open an Idea issue with the screen name, the old words and your version.

rounds.name: Round 1: first impressions and finding things
rounds.who: 12 to 15 young people across the quotas, plus 4 parents or carers and 4 youth workers or teachers

rounds.name: Round 2: accessibility, languages and sign languages
rounds.who: 8 to 10 people, at least 4 d/Deaf or disabled and at least 2 Welsh, Gaelic or Irish speakers

rounds.name: Round 3: direction of travel
rounds.who: 15 to 20 people, including youth councils and MYPs through their organisations

sign_up.status_when_empty: Signing up for research is paused. Before anyone your age takes part, Amplify needs a named safeguarding lead (the adult responsible for keeping you safe) and a written plan for what happens if something worries us (readiness gate G06, open items O12 and O14). Until both are in place we are not asking anyone to sign up, so please do not post that you want to take part. If you already took part, you can still withdraw what you said at any time with the contact form: give only your session code.
sign_up.group_route: Group sessions are paused too, for the same reason. Once a safeguarding lead is in place, schools, youth councils and youth groups will be able to take part as a group: one adult registers and tells us roughly how many and what ages. We then send the participant information to that adult, and sessions run in your setting under your safeguarding policy.

promise: Taking part is voluntary. You can stop at any time, skip any question and withdraw what you said within 30 days, without giving a reason.
Under 16s take part only with a parent's or carer's consent as well as their own. For 16 and 17 year olds we ask a parent or carer to be told, unless that would put the young person at risk.
No one under 18 is ever in a session alone with a researcher. A parent, carer, teacher or youth worker is present or close by, and every facilitator has a background check (DBS, PVG or AccessNI).
We recruit young people through trusted organisations and parents, never by messaging them directly online.
Nothing is run through anyone who makes decisions about you: your answers are never shared with your school, employer or service.
Contact details stay in the private form service and are deleted when you leave the panel or after 12 months without contact. They are never put on GitHub, on the portal or in any report.
Everyone is thanked at the same rate, with a voucher that does not affect benefits, and travel and support costs are paid up front.
Interpreters (BSL, ISL, Welsh, Gaelic) and other support are booked before a session is offered. You can answer by speaking, typing, drawing, signing or with a supporter.
You see what we concluded, in a format that works for you, before anyone else does.
If you tell us something that makes us worried about your safety, we will follow safeguarding procedures and tell you what we are doing.

young: I know what this research is about and what I will be asked to do.
I know I can stop at any time, skip questions, and change my mind within 30 days.
I know my name will not be used in anything published.
I agree to being recorded (optional: you can take part without this).
parent: I have read (or had read to me) the information about this research.
I understand my child can stop at any time, and that they can withdraw within 30 days.
I understand a trusted adult will be present or close by throughout, and facilitators are background-checked.
I consent to my child taking part.
I consent to the session being recorded (optional).
consent.keep: We take notes using a session code, never a name. Recordings are made only with consent and deleted within 30 days; notes are deleted after 6 months. Findings are published as themes and totals only.

England; Scotland; Wales; Northern Ireland; prefer not to say

quotas.group: Young people in each of the four nations
Each age band: 11 to 13, 14 to 15, 16 to 17, 18 to 25
Care-experienced young people and young carers
Young people in rural areas or with poor connectivity
Young people from minority ethnic communities
Young people not in education, employment or training
Youth workers, teachers and club leaders

quotas_note: Minimums, not targets. Protected characteristics are recorded only as totals, never against a person.

sessions.title: Usability session for young people (40 minutes)

steps.detail: Introductions, check the trusted adult is present or nearby, consent (young person and, for under 16s, parent), access needs, permission to record.
Something you'd change about your area or school, and who you'd tell.

1. Find a way to take part that fits your age and nation. 2. Find who to talk to if you're worried about something. 3. Use a tooltip to find out what an MYP is. 4. Find a free coding club. 5. Change the explainer to suit you. 6. Find how to suggest an idea.
Easiest and hardest thing; one thing to change. Thank you, and how you'll hear what changed.

sessions.note: Record: completed (yes, with help, no), the words people used and where they hesitated. Don't help unless asked or stuck for 2 minutes.

sessions.title: Accessibility session (45 to 60 minutes)

steps.detail: Consent; the person shows their set-up; agree how they'll share what they hear or see; interpreter introductions.
Three tasks from the usability session, using their own technology or language. Note every barrier and workaround.
What would make the biggest difference? Anything that would stop you using it?

sessions.note: Severity: blocks (cannot complete), slows (completes with effort), annoys. Blockers become must-fix items straight away.

sessions.title: Co-design workshop in a school or youth group (75 minutes)

steps.detail: Ground rules agreed together; consent; how ideas will be used and credited (first names or nicknames only, if wanted).
Share what we've learned so far; agree the need in one sentence in the group's own words.
Sketch, write, draw or act out ideas; share and group them. Any way of contributing counts.
Dot-vote the top ideas on how much they help, who they include and how hard they are.
What goes into the backlog, and when and how the group will hear back.

sessions.note: Run by the group's own staff with a facilitator; breaks every 25 minutes; materials sent three working days before.

sessions.title: Design crit (30 to 45 minutes)

steps.detail: What the design is for, who it's for, and what kind of feedback is wanted.
What works, what's confusing, what's missing. Feedback is on the work, never the person.
Agree the top three changes and who will make them; credit everyone who contributed.

sessions.note: Designs by under 18s are shared without names, faces or school logos.

findings.theme: Many young people cannot use GitHub: accounts are for 13 and over.
findings.change: An assisted route through a trusted adult, and age guidance on every contribution route

findings.theme: Different readers need different explanations of the same screen.
findings.change: Tooltips everywhere and an explainer bar tailored to eight personas

findings.theme: Girls and young women remain under-represented in STEM, especially engineering and technology.
findings.change: A STEM spotlight with free opportunities and a DevOps path

findings.theme: Under 16s will face more restrictions on social media.
findings.evidence: Government plans, noted on What's new
findings.change: Sharing routes labelled for adults and allies acting on a young person's behalf

synthesis: Write up within two weeks of the last session in a round.
Group notes into themes; count sessions per theme; rate severity (blocks, slows, annoys).
Fix anything that excludes a group first.
Turn each theme into a backlog item or a change, with the finding's id.
Show participants what we concluded, in their format, before publishing.
Publish the summary here, update You said, we did, and close the loop with the groups who took part.

groups.purpose: Young people who review designs, words and new features before they ship.

groups.name: Accessibility and inclusion
groups.purpose: Assistive technology, plain English, easy read, rural and low-bandwidth access.

groups.name: Languages and sign languages
groups.purpose: What to translate or sign first, and checking it with native speakers and signers.

groups.name: Research
groups.purpose: Plan rounds, recruit across the quotas through trusted organisations, synthesise and publish findings.

groups.name: Safeguarding review
groups.purpose: Youth workers and safeguarding leads who check every route that involves young people.

group_terms: Open to anyone who agrees to the code of conduct; under 18s join through a school, youth group or with a parent or carer.
About an hour a month: one online meeting at a time that suits young people (after school), and work in your own time.
Decisions are recorded on a GitHub issue, never only in a call. Nothing that identifies a member is published.
A convenor keeps notes and actions; the role rotates every 6 months.

benchmark.name: System Usability Scale
benchmark.credit: System Usability Scale by John Brooke (1986), free to use with attribution.
items: I think that I would like to use Amplify often.
I thought Amplify was easy to use.
I think that I would need the support of someone technical to be able to use Amplify.
I found the various parts of Amplify were well joined up.
I thought there was too much inconsistency in Amplify.
I would imagine that most people would learn to use Amplify very quickly.
I found Amplify very awkward to use.
I felt very confident using Amplify.
I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with Amplify.
benchmark.scoring: Odd statements score the answer minus 1; even statements score 5 minus the answer (answers 1 to 5). Add the ten and multiply by 2.5 for a score from 0 to 100.
benchmark.reading: Scores are compared between rounds, not against a pass mark. Published research puts the average across many products at about 68.
